t: Greek has the longest recorded history of any living Indo-European language, from the Mycenaean tablets of the 14th century BCE through the classical language of Athens to the Greek spoken today.

It was the language of Homer, the Athenian dramatists, historians and philosophers, and, after Alexander’s conquests, as the Koine or “common” Greek, the shared language of the eastern Mediterranean and of the New Testament.

Its alphabet, the first to write vowels as well as consonants, became the model of the Latin and Cyrillic alphabets, and its words supply the terms of science, medicine, philosophy and politics in languages across the world.
dyk: The oldest Greek writing survived by accident: the Linear B tablets were records of unbaked clay, meant to be reused, until the fires that destroyed the palaces of Knossos and Pylos baked them hard.
ev: Scribes at Knossos record Mycenaean Greek in the Linear B script
The Greeks adapt the Phoenician alphabet, adding letters for vowels
The Iliad and the Odyssey take shape, the oldest works of Greek literature
Athens officially adopts the Ionic alphabet of twenty-four letters
Alexander the Great begins the conquests that carry Greek to Egypt, Persia and India
The Hebrew scriptures are translated into Greek in Alexandria: the Septuagint
Manuel Chrysoloras begins teaching Greek in Florence, reviving its study in western Europe
Greece makes Demotic, the popular form of the language, its official language

f.family: Indo-European: the Hellenic branch, of which Greek is the only surviving language
f.script: The Greek alphabet, adapted from the Phoenician in the 8th century BCE; earlier the Mycenaean syllabic script Linear B
f.earliest: Linear B tablets from Knossos and Pylos, 14th and 13th centuries BCE; alphabetic inscriptions from the 8th century BCE
f.status: Continued as Medieval and Modern Greek, spoken today by about 13 million people; ancient Greek is still read in schools and used in Orthodox worship
